title: Long Mott (Dow / X-energy): (PUBLIC) DRAFT SE Chapter 8 - LMGS CPA - Plant Programs [['Safety Evaluation']]

documents.text:
OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


THIS NRC STAFF DRAFT SE HAS BEEN PREPARED AND IS BEING RELEASED TO SUPPORT
INTERACTIONS WITH THE ACRS. THIS DRAFT SE HAS NOT BEEN SUBJECT TO FULL NRC
MANAGEMENT AND LEGAL REVIEWS AND APPROVALS, AND ITS CONTENTS SHOULD NOT BE
INTERPRETED AS OFFICIAL AGENCY POSITIONS.


8     Plant Programs
This chapter of the safety evaluation (SE) describes the NRC staff’s review and evaluation of
the Long Mott Generating Station's (LMGS) preliminary safety analysis report (PSAR) chapter 8,
“Plant Programs,” which provides an overview of plant programs relied upon to support the
Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) 18-04 process, addressing the purpose, scope, and performance
objectives as well as applicability to safety-related (SR) structures, systems, and components
(SSCs), non-safety-related with special treatment (NSRST) SSCs, and operations activities. The
PSAR states that details of operational programs and special treatments will be provided in the
final safety analysis report (FSAR) as part of the application for an operating license (OL). 10
CFR 50.34(b)(6) requires information concerning facility operations to be included in the FSAR
that a holder of a construction permit (CP) would submit when requesting an OL. Accordingly,
the NRC staff's review of operational programs to be used to assure safe operation would take
place as part of NRC staff's review of the OL application.
8.1       Quality Assurance Program and Reliability Assurance Program
PSAR section 8.1 describes the quality assurance program (QAP) and references topical report,
“Long Mott Energy, LLC Quality Assurance Program Description,” (hereafter referred to as the
Long Mott Energy (LME) QAPD) (ML24345A043).
PSAR section 8.1.4 describes the LMGS reliability assurance program (RAP) that applies to SR
and NSRST SSCs.
The applicable regulatory requirements for the evaluation of the QAP and RAP are as follows:
      •    Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) 50.34(a)(7);

      •    10 CFR Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,”
           Appendix B, “Quality Assurance Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants and Fuel
           Reprocessing Plants.”
The applicable guidance for the evaluation of QAP and RAP is as follows:
      •    DANU-ISG-2022-01, “Review of Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Advanced Reactor
           Applications—Roadmap,” section 4, “Quality Assurance Plan,” (ML23277A139).

      •    Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.233, “Guidance for a Technology-Inclusive, Risk-Informed, and
           Performance-Based Methodology to Inform the Licensing Basis and Content of
           Applications for Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Non-Light Water Reactors”
           (ML20091L698), which endorses Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) 18-04, “Risk-Informed
           Performance-Based Technology-Inclusive Guidance for Non-Light Water Reactor
           Licensing Basis Development,” Revision 1 (ML19241A472).



                                                  8-8

                      OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


   •    NUREG-0800, “Standard Review Plan (SRP) for the Review of Safety Analysis Reports
        for Nuclear Power Plants,” section 17.4, “Reliability Assurance Program,” Revision 1
        (ML13296A435), and section 17.5, “Quality Assurance Program Description – Design
        Certification, Early Site Permit and New License Applicants,” Revision 1
        (ML15037A441).

   •    SRM-SECY-95-132, “Policy and Technical Issues Associated with the Regulatory
        Treatment of Non-Safety Systems (RTNSS) in Passive Plant Designs.”
PSAR section 5.3 provides definitions of principal design criteria (PDC). The NRC staff identified
the QAP as a key part of meeting PDC 1, “Quality Standards and Records.” PDC 1 is applicable
to all safety-significant SSCs (i.e., SR and NSRST SSCs) and how LME has applied the QAP in
meeting PDC 1 is described in PSAR sections 6.4 and 7.3 and evaluated in sections 6.4 and 7.3
of this SE.
8.1.1   Technical Evaluation
8.1.1.1 QA Program
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.1 and the LME QAPD, which is incorporated by
reference in PSAR table 1.4-4. The NRC staff approved the LME QAPD for use with a CP
application subject to two limitations (ML25269A117). LME addressed the limitations associated
with QAPD TR in PSAR table 1.4-8. The NRC staff evaluation of PSAR table 1.4-8 is presented
in SE section 1.4.
The LME QAPD established the QAP at LMGS. Within the QAP, the SSC are divided into
categories based on safety classification (e.g., SR, NSRST) which determines the treatment of
the safety-significant SSC. The NRC staff will verify implementation of the QAP as part of the
NRC advanced reactor construction oversight program.
PSAR section 8.1.2, “Systems, Structures, and Components Classification,” summarizes SSC
classification and associated quality assurance (QA) guidance provided in NEI 18-04. The NRC
staff finds this summary acceptable because it is consistent with NEI 18-04, which is endorsed
by RG 1.233.
PSAR section 8.1.3, “Determination of the QA Program Requirements,” summarizes QA
program requirements and states, in part, that “SR SSCs QA requirements are consistent with
the LME QAPD, Part I and Part II” and “NSRST SSCs QA requirements are consistent with the
LME QAPD, Part III. Additional QA requirements, up to and including NQA-1, may be applied to
NSRST SSCs as a special treatment consistent with non-safety related QA program guidance
through the NEI 18-04 Integrated Decision-Making Process (IDP).” Since the QA treatment for
SR SSCs is consistent with 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix B and QA treatment for NSRST SSCs is
at a minimum consistent with the LME QAPD and expanded with NEI 18-04 special treatments,
as endorsed by RG 1.233, the NRC staff determined that the QA program requirements
summarized in PSAR section 8.1.3 are acceptable.
8.1.1.2 Reliability Assurance Program
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.1.4, which describes the RAP, in accordance with the
associated acceptance criteria within the context of applicability to LMGS’ specific reactor


                                               8-9

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


technology in SRP 17.4. Specifically, the NRC staff reviewed the RAP to determine whether it
adequately considers the following attributes:
   •   Describe the RAP used during the design including its scope, purpose, and objectives.
   •   Evaluate and prioritize the SSCs in the design, based on their degree of risk
       significance.
   •   List SSCs designated as risk significant.
   •   For those SSCs designated as risk significant, determine:
           o Dominant failure modes that consider industry experience and analytical models.
           o Key assumptions and risk insights from probabilistic, deterministic, or other
               methods that consider operations, maintenance, and monitoring activities.
The NRC staff determined that the applicant included a description of the details of the design
reliability assurance program (D-RAP) that will be implemented during the design, procurement,
fabrication, construction, and preoperational testing activities preceding initial fuel load. The
applicant’s description included a discussion of the scope, purpose, objectives, framework, and
those activities that will occur in the two phases of the D-RAP (i.e., detailed plant design and
detailed plant design following issuance of an OL). The NRC staff confirmed that the scope,
purpose, and objectives of the applicant’s D-RAP provide sufficient detail for the preliminary
design and are consistent with subsection I of SRP section 17.4, Revision 1. Based on its
review, the NRC staff finds the description of the D-RAP to be acceptable.
The NRC staff determined that the applicant has established and applied the appropriate
D-RAP programmatic controls to support design and construction activities. Consistent with
guidance in SRP section 17.4, Revision 1, the programmatic controls established by the
applicant address organization responsibilities, design control activities, procedures and
instructions, records control, corrective actions, and audit plans. Based on its review, the NRC
staff finds that the applicant has established adequate programmatic controls for the D-RAP.
The NRC staff determined that the applicant’s methodology for identifying the SSCs within the
scope of the RAP is based on risk-informed performance-based methodology for design and
licensing basis development from NEI 18-04. The methodology provides an objective and
repeatable approach to identify SSCs within the scope of the RAP. The applicant’s methodology
is consistent with the practice for identifying risk-significant SSCs, as discussed in RG 1.233.
This methodology is consistent with that described in SRP section 17.4, Revision 1. Based on
the NRC staff’s review, the NRC staff finds that the applicant has established an adequate
methodology for identifying RAP SSCs.
The NRC staff determined that the applicant uses an integrated decision-making process (IDP)
and the integrated decision-making process panel (IDPP) as described in NEI 18-04 to evaluate
the adequacy of defense-in-depth (DID) and the safety classification of SSCs, which includes
determining which SSCs are categorized as NSRST based on risk significance. The roles and
responsibilities, decision-making attributes, and actions to establish DID from the IDPP and the
IDP are described in NEI 18-04, section 5.9, “Risk-Informed and Performance-Based Evaluation
of DID Adequacy.” The NRC staff verified that the description of the IDPP is consistent with that
described in SRP section 17.4, Revision 1. Based on the NRC staff’s review, the NRC staff finds
the description and implementation of the IDPP to be acceptable.



                                              8-10

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                       OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


Overall, the NRC staff determined that the application contains a comprehensive list of SSCs
subject to RAP requirements consistent with the state of the plant design and PRA at the time of
CP application and the list of RAP SSCs based on the methodology for identifying and
characterizing SSCs is within the scope of the RAP. The lists in PSAR chapter 5, “PRA Safety
Functions, Design Criteria, and SSC Classification,” sufficiently identify the RAP SSCs classified
as SR and NSRST that are needed to meet risk targets, and PSAR chapter 6, “Safety-related
SSC Criteria and Capabilities,” and chapter 7, “Non-Safety-Related with Special Treatment
Structures, Systems, and Components Criteria and Capabilities,” include the basis for including
each SSC in the RAP in PSAR chapters 6 and 7, respectively, for SR and NSRST SSCs.
Consistent with SRP section 17.4, Revision 1, the NRC staff finds that the applicant
appropriately cited PSAR chapters 6 and 7 that describe the SSC boundaries. Based on the
NRC staff’s review, the NRC staff finds the RAP SSCs list to be acceptable.
The NRC staff determined that the application describes a proposed process for determining
dominant failure modes of RAP SSCs. Consistent with guidance in SRP section 17.4,
Revision 1, the applicant’s proposed process for determining dominant failure modes
incorporates consideration of insights from the PRA model, analytical methods, and industry
experience. The process described by the applicant is consistent with the guidance for an
acceptable process described in SRP section 17.4, Revision 1, and therefore is acceptable.
The NRC staff determined that the applicant specified where the QA controls for design
activities are described. The applicant cited the LME QAPD, which describes QA controls
applied to non-safety-related RAP SSCs. The QA controls are evaluated in the NRC staff’s SE
of LME QAPD. These controls are consistent with the NRC staff’s expectations for QA controls
described in SRP section 17.4, Revision 1, and are therefore acceptable.
8.1.2    Conclusion
Based on the NRC staff’s review, the NRC staff finds that the QAP, as described in PSAR
section 8.1 and in the LME QAPD is consistent with the applicable regulatory guidance and,
therefore, meets the regulatory requirements identified in 10 CFR 50.34(a)(7) for the issuance of
a CP. The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.1.4 in accordance with Item E of SECY-95-132
and SRP section 17.4, Revision 1, and concludes that the D-RAP program as described in the
PSAR is acceptable to demonstrate that it follows SRP section 17.4, revision 1 because the
plant is designed, to be constructed, and to be operated in a manner that is consistent with the
risk insights and key assumptions from the probabilistic and deterministic analyses.
8.2     Reliability and Integrity Management Program
PSAR section 8.2 describes the reliability and integrity management (RIM) program which will
be implemented in accordance with American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Section
XI, Division 2, “Requirements for Reliability and Integrity Management (RIM) Programs for
Nuclear Power Plants,” as endorsed in RG 1.246, “Acceptability of ASME Code, Section XI,
Division 2, ‘Requirements for Reliability and Integrity Management (RIM) Programs for Nuclear
Power Plants,’ for Non-Light Water Reactors,” Revision 0 (ML22111A087). The objectives of the
RIM program are to define, evaluate, and implement strategies to ensure that the facility risk
and reliability goals (i.e. reliability targets) for each passive SSC whose failure could adversely
affect facility safety and reliability are defined, achieved, and maintained throughout the facility
lifetime through a combination of monitoring, examination, tests, operation and maintenance
programs.
                                                     8-11

                      OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


The applicable guidance for the evaluation of RIM is as follows:
   •    RG 1.246
The NRC staff identified the RIM program as a key part of meeting the following PDCs. How
LME has applied the RIM program in meeting these PDCs for specific SSCs is described in
PSAR sections 6.4 and 7.3 and evaluated in sections 6.4 and 7.3 of this SE. Since there are no
requirements for inservice inspection (ISI) applicable to CPs, these PDCs are not addressed
below:
   •    PDC 4, “Environmental and Dynamic Effects Design Basis”;
   •    PDC 6, “Monitoring, Inspection, Testing, and Surveillance”; and
   •    PDC 14, “Reactor Helium Pressure Boundary”
8.2.1   Technical Evaluation
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.2, in which the applicant stated that the RIM program
will be developed following the 2019 Edition of AMSE Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section
XI, Division 2 (ASME.XI.2) and will be implemented in accordance with RG 1.246, which
endorses the use of RIM. In addition, the RIM program will follow the associated code case N-
954-1, “Requirements for Monitoring and Nondestructive Examination (MANDE) of Graphite
Core Components in a High-Temperature Gas Reactor.” Code Case N-954-1 is not endorsed in
the current revision of RG 1.246. The NRC staff reviewed the approaches in N-954-1 to develop
the monitoring and non-destructive examination (MANDE) for graphite core components. LME's
approach is acceptable because N-954-1 provides technically sound guidance on establishing
appropriate MANDE for degradation mechanisms relevant to graphite materials in high
temperature gas reactors (HTGRs).
As described in ASME.XI.2, the RIM program scope shall include applicable SSCs whose
failure could adversely affect plant safety and reliability. The RIM program requires conducting a
degradation mechanism assessment for each component in the scope of the RIM program,
determining the reliability targets for the SSCs, and identifying RIM strategies to ensure
reliability targets can be met. The objective of the RIM program is to ensure that passive
components within the RIM program scope achieve an acceptable level of reliability to support
the plant probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) throughout the life of the plant. The RIM program
involves design interaction, performance monitoring, inspections, tests, maintenance, and
replacements, as strategies to ensure the SSCs achieve an acceptable level of reliability to
support the LMGS PRA.
The NRC staff reviewed the applicant’s preliminary RIM program scope and the criteria used by
the applicant to determine which SSCs are included in the RIM program as described in PSAR
section 8.2. The applicant states that the RIM program scope includes SR and risk-significant
NSRST passive SSCs but does not include NSRST SSCs relied on for DID The preliminary RIM
program scope departs from the scope requirement in ASME BPVC XI-2 that requires passive
SSCs whose failure could adversely affect plant safety and reliability to be included in the RIM
program; under ASME BPVC XI-2, NSRST SSCs relied on for DID would be included. The NRC
staff did not make any findings on program scope but notes that a final program scope,
including a basis for the departure from ASME BPVC XI-2, as endorsed by RG 1.246, will be
reviewed at the OL application stage.

                                              8-12

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                       OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.2.2 which describes the preliminary degradation
mechanism assessment (DMA). The applicant states that considerations such as material
selection, service conditions, and operating environment will be evaluated. Existing operational
and test data is used to inform material selection. ASME XI-2 Article VII-3 “High Temperature
Gas-Reactor-Type Facilities” provides requirements for identifying and evaluating potentially
active degradation mechanisms specific to HTGR facilities. In addition, while not explicitly stated
in the PSAR section 8.2.2, the results of the materials qualification program described in PSAR
section 3.8 and the research and development program described in chapter 13, “Research and
Development Program,” will also inform the DMA and associated selection of MANDE
strategies. The NRC staff did not make any findings on the preliminary considerations for the
DMA because 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6) requires information concerning facility operations to be
included in the FSAR that a holder of a CP would submit when requesting an OL. The NRC staff
notes that ASME XI-2.VII-3 is approved for evaluating the DMA, with conditions, in RG 1.246.
The NRC staff did not make findings on the remainder of PSAR section 8.2, including 1) the
acceptability of the reliability target allocation or confirmation process of the preliminary
reliability targets, 2) preliminary RIM strategies and evaluation of uncertainties, or 3) preservice
inspection. The NRC staff expects the applicant to provide the final reliability targets and RIM
strategies for SSCs that are in the RIM program, including the technical basis on how the
reliability targets are derived and met, and consideration of uncertainties, in the FSAR
supporting an OL application.
8.2.2    Conclusion
The NRC staff will review the RIM program at the OL application stage as required by 10 CFR
50.34(b)(6)(iv). Due to the preliminary nature of the program, the applicant is not seeking to
demonstrate compliance with this regulation at the CP application stage. The NRC staff is not
making any regulatory findings pertaining to the contents of the RIM program meeting the
requirements of ASME BPVC XI-2, as conditioned in RG 1.246 because 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6)
requires information concerning facility operations to be included in the FSAR that a holder of a
CP would submit when requesting an OL. The NRC staff will evaluate the RIM program as part
of the OL application review, including the basis and acceptability of the departure from the
scope of ASME Section XI-2 as endorsed in RG 1.246, which includes NSRST SSCs relied on
for DID.
8.3     Maintenance Program
PSAR section 8.3 provides a high-level description of the maintenance program. The stated
objectives of the program are to control the performance of maintenance activities in the
plantand the program is applied to passive and active safety-significant SSCs.
PSAR section 8.3 describes the program for maintenance activities for passive and active
safety-significant SSCs addressed by 10 CFR 50.65. The NRC staff notes that the applicant has
identified appropriate guidance documents for maintenance activities. However, the NRC staff is
not making any regulatory findings in this SE because, per 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6)(iv), plans for
conduct of normal operations, including maintenance, surveillance, and periodic testing of SSCs
are applicable at the OL application stage. For this reason and because the applicant is not
seeking to demonstrate compliance with this regulation at the CP application stage consistent


                                                8-13

                      OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


with 10 CFR 50.34(a)(7), the NRC staff is not making any regulatory findings pertaining to this
section.
While the NRC staff did not make any regulatory findings pertaining to the maintenance
program described in the PSAR, the NRC staff reviewed the approach discussed in developing
the maintenance program and has the following observations. The NRC staff notes that LME is
using the maintenance program in lieu of the inservice testing (IST) program for NSRST SSCs
relied on for DID but has not provided information on how diagnostic testing would be
performed. In addition, while an SSC could be in scope for both the IST and maintenance
programs under 50.65, the regulations and purpose of the programs are separate. The NRC
staff will evaluate the maintenance program as part of the OL application review, including the
basis and acceptability of having separate IST programs as well as the program for performing
diagnostic testing of NSRST SSCs relied on for DID.
8.4   Inservice Testing Program
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.4, which states that an IST program will be established
to meet the intent of the requirements in 10 CFR 50.55a(f). The PSAR states that the IST
program shall “fulfill the intent of the requirements of 10 CFR 50.55a(f)” and the “IST program is
implemented in accordance with ASME Operation and Maintenance OM-2 Code, “Component
Testing Requirements at Nuclear Facilities,” 2024 Edition (OM-2-2024). The PSAR states that
the IST program is applied to active SR and risk-significant NSRST SSCs. In RG 1.220,
“Acceptability of ASME OM-2 Code, Component Testing Requirements at Nuclear Facilities”
(ML25329A088), the NRC staff endorsed ASME OM-2-2024 as an acceptable method for
implementing an IST program. While OM-2 does not specify a scope for the IST program, the
NRC staff notes that it may be applied to any active SSCs and allows for a graded IST
approach. The NRC staff notes that the applicant has chosen to use the maintenance program
rather than the IST program to ensure functional capability of safety-significant SSCs for active
components. The NRC staff also noted the maintenance program activities may include
exercise and diagnostic testing which traditionally belong to the IST program. The NRC staff is
not making any regulatory findings in this SE pertaining to this section or the acceptability of the
applicant’s approach to use its maintenance program to meet the requirements for an in-service
testing program, as required by 10 CFR 50.55a(f) for an OL, because the requirements in 10
CFR 50.34(b)(6)(iv) are not applicable to a CP application and the applicant is not seeking to
demonstrate compliance with this regulation at the CP application stage.
8.5   Environmental Qualification Program
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.5, which describes the program for qualification of the
safety-significant electrical equipment in systems addressed by 10 CFR 50.49(b). The NRC staff
notes that the applicant has identified appropriate guidance documents for environmental
qualification of safety-significant electrical equipment. However, the NRC staff is not making any
regulatory findings pertaining to this section because, per 10 CFR 50.49(a), the requirements in
10 CFR 50.49 are not applicable to a CP application and the applicant is not seeking to
demonstrate compliance with this regulation at the CP application stage (i.e., the application
does not include all the information required by 10 CFR 50.49). PDC 4, “Environmental and
Dynamic Effects Design Basis,” states that, “safety-significant structures, systems, and
components shall be designed to accommodate the effects of, and to be compatible with, the
environmental conditions associated with normal operation, maintenance, testing, anticipated
                                               8-14

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                       OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


operational occurrences, design basis events, and design basis accidents commensurate with
the safety-significance of the functions to be performed.” The NRC staff’s evaluations of the
design bases for SR and NSRST SSCs with respect to addressing the requirements of PDC 4
are provided in chapters 6 and 7 of this SE.
8.6       Fire Protection Program
The NRC staff reviewed the preliminary design of the fire protection program (FPP) described in
the LMGS PSAR to assess the adequacy of the design in support of the issuance of a CP.
The applicable regulatory requirements for the evaluation of fire protection for a CP are:
      •    10 CFR 50.34(a)(3)(i)
The applicable guidance for the evaluation of fire protection is:
      •    RG 1.189, “Fire Protection for Nuclear Power Plants,” Revision 5 (ML23214A287); and
      •    RG 1.191, “Fire Protection Program for Nuclear Power Plants During Decommissioning
           and Permanent Shutdown.” Revision 1 (ML20287A199).
Definitions of PDCs are included in PSAR section 5.3. The NRC staff identified the FPP as a
key part of meeting PDC 3, “Fire Protection.” How LME has applied the FPP in meeting PDC 3
for specific SSCs is described in PSAR sections 6.4 and 7.3 and evaluated in sections 6.4 and
7.3 of this SE.
8.6.1      Technical Evaluation
The NRC staff evaluated the sufficiency of the facility’s preliminary fire protection systems and
programs as described in the PSAR as required by PDC 3.
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 1.1.4.3.9 which states that the fire protection systems
consist of:
•     the nuclear island fire protection (NIFP) system, which provides fire protection for SSCs
      located within nuclear island buildings and structures;
•     the conventional island fire protection (CIFP) system, which provides fire protection for the
      conventional island SSCs; and
•     the plant fire protection system, which stores, supplies, and distributes fire water to the
      NIFP and CIFP systems.
The applicant states that these systems are one part of the overall FPP designed and
maintained to meet the requirements of PDC 3 and that other parts of the FPP include
procedures, analyses, administrative controls, personnel, and other support programs. The
NRC staff also reviewed PSAR section 1.1.4.4.10 in which the applicant describes the fire
protection pump house and fire water storage tank structure. The applicant states that these
structures provide adequate space for water supply and redundant water pumps for fire
protection purposes at LMGS. The applicant also stated that the pump house contains the
diesel fuel storage tank. The NRC staff evaluated the information in PSAR sections 1.1.4.3.9
and 1.1.4.4.10 and finds that the level of detail in these sections is acceptable for a preliminary
design.
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR table 1.4-2 in which the applicant indicates that the final FPP will
fully conform with the portions of RG 1.189 that are technically relevant to the applicant’s non-
light water reactor (LWR) design. Portions of the RG that are determined to be not technically
                                                  8-15

                      OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                    OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


relevant will have alternatives identified and justified in the FSAR. In PSAR section 8.6 the
applicant states that deviations from RG 1.189 will be justified in the OL application. PSAR table
1.4-2 also indicates that the guidance provided in RG 1.191 will be addressed at the OL
application stage. The NRC staff evaluated this information and determined that conformance
with these RGs is not required during the preliminary design phase. Based on the NRC staff’s
evaluation, the NRC staff finds that the descriptions in the PSAR are acceptable because
conformance with these RGs will be addressed at the OL application stage.
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR table 1.4-3 in which the applicant lists a selection of codes and
standards related to fire protection and building construction that will be used for LMGS,
including those from the American Society of Testing Materials, the Institute of Electrical and
Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), and
Underwriters Laboratories. The NRC staff reviewed the table and determined that the applicant
included well established consensus codes and standards related to fire protection and building
construction that they intend to follow during design and construction of the facility. Based on
the NRC staff’s review, the NRC staff finds the information provided in the PSAR regarding
codes and standards acceptable for a preliminary design.
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 6.1.1 in which the applicant states that the design basis
internal fire hazard has not been evaluated for the preliminary design but will be evaluated at
the OL application stage. The NRC staff evaluated this section of the PSAR and finds that this
information is acceptable for a preliminary design because an evaluation of the design basis
internal fire hazard is not required at the CP stage and the applicant states that the design basis
internal fire hazards will be evaluated at the OL application stage.
The NRC staff reviewed the introductory sections of PSAR chapters 6 and 7, in which the
applicant states that, consistent with PDC 3, safety-significant SSCs would be designed and
located to minimize the probability and effect of fires and explosions consistent with other safety
requirements and the safety significance of the functions to be performed. The applicant also
states that non-combustible and fire-resistant materials will be used wherever practical
throughout, particularly in locations with safety-significant SSCs. Finally, the applicant states
that fire detection and fighting systems will be: of appropriate capacity and capability; provided
and designed to minimize the adverse effects of fires on safety-significant SSCs commensurate
with the safety significance of their functions; and designed to ensure that their rupture or
inadvertent operation does not significantly impair the safety capability of these SSCs. The NRC
staff evaluated this information and determined the design and location of these SSCs would
meet the requirements of PDC 3. Based on its evaluation, the NRC staff finds that the
information provided in the PSAR regarding design and location of SSCs is appropriate for a
preliminary design because the SSCs would conform to the requirements of PDC 3.
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.6 in which the applicant describes the elements of the
FPP and states that the details will be developed for the OL application. These elements
include:
   •   Fire detection and suppression systems;
   •   Plant and system design and layout, including use of fire resistant assemblies (e.g., fire
       barriers, fire doors, fire dampers);
   •   Engineering analyses, including a fire hazards analysis and safe shutdown analysis;
   •   Administrative controls, policies and procedures;
   •   Organization and staffing; and
                                               8-16

                   OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
                        OFFICIAL USE ONLY – PROPRIETARY INFORMATION


      •   Support programs (quality assurance, inspection and testing, maintenance, and
          training).
The applicant further states that the operational FPP will be in conformance with the technically
relevant portions of RG 1.189, Revision 5. The applicant also states that the FPP will conform
with the provisions of NFPA Standard 804 that are technically relevant to post-fire safe
shutdown capability and mitigation of a radiological release resulting from a fire. Finally, the
applicant states that justification for any portions of the FPP that require deviation or alternate
methodologies from RG 1.189 or NFPA 804 will be provided in the OL application.
The NRC staff evaluated the information provided by the applicant in PSAR section 8.6 and

8.9.1   Technical Evaluation
PSAR table 1.4-2 states that the LMGS CVAP fully conforms with RG 1.20, Revision 4.
Accordingly, the NRC staff reviewed the PSAR against the guidance in RG 1.20.
RG 1.20 section C.1 requires that the applicant classify its reactor internal configurations as
prototype, limited prototype, or non-prototype. During audit discussion, LME stated that the
reactor internals of the first Xe-100 reactor module are classified as prototype. LME also stated
that upon the successful implementation of the CVAP for the first XE-100 module, the
subsequent three modules can be classified as non-prototype for purposes of vibration
assessment. The NRC staff findings about the LMGS classification of reactor internals for the
purpose of CVAP plan are summarized below:
   •    RG 1.20 section C.1.1 defines a “protoype” as a configuration of reactor internals that
        represents a first-of-a-kind or unique design because of the arrangement, design, size,
        or operating conditions. LMGS classification for the reactor internals of the first Xe-100
        module as prototype is consistent with the guidance in RG 1.20 and is thus acceptable.
   •    RG 1.20 section C.1.1 states that after the NRC staff accepts the prototype design and
        the CVAP is completed with no adverse vibration or excessive loading, the prototype
        reactor internals are classified as a “valid prototype.” RG 1.20 section C.1.3 further
        states that reactor internals that have substantially the same arrangement, design, size,
        and operating conditions as a “valid prototype” can be classified as a “non-prototype.”
        Since the three subsequent LMGS reactor modules are expected to have similar
        arrangement, design, size, and operating conditions as the protype (i.e., the first LMGS
        reactor module unit), the NRC staff finds that the classification of non-prototype reactor
        internals of the three subsequent LMGS modules is consistent with the guidance in RG
        1.20, if the CVAP for the first LMGS module will be successfully completed and the NRC
        staff accepts the prototype design. In the review of OL application, the NRC staff will
        confirm that the CVAP for the prototype reactor internals is successfully completed such

8.9.2   Conclusion
Based on the information provided in PSAR section 8.9, the NRC staff determined that the
methods and procedures for developing the scope, approach, and stages of report for the RVI
CVAP are consistent with RG 1.20. RG 1.20 provides an acceptable approach to quantitatively
demonstrate that there were no adverse vibration phenomena or excessive loading to impact
structural integrity of the reactor internals. Complying with RG 1.20 thus satisfies the
requirements in PDC 4 to protect safety-significant SSCs from dynamic effects. RG 1.20 also
provides guidance to appropriately document the CVAP plan and results. By complying with RG
1.20, section C.2.4, the LMGS CVAP plan satisfies the requirements of PDC 1 to maintain
appropriate records of the design and testing of safety-significant SSCs. By supporting
requirements in PDCs 1 and 4, the LMGS CVAP in PSAR section 8.9 satisfies the requirements
in 10 CFR 50.34 (a)(3)(i) and (a)(3)(ii). Therefore, the NRC staff concludes that the RVI CVAP
program as described in the PSAR, provides reasonable assurance that the applicable
regulatory requirements and guidance for the issuance of a CP are met and additional details of
the CVAP can be left for consideration in the FSAR.
8.10 Reliability, Availability, and Maintainability Program
The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.10, which provides a high-level description of the
reliability, availability, and maintenance (RAM) program. The PSAR states the objectives of the
program are to define, evaluate, and implement strategies to ensure that reliability, availability,
and maintainability of passive SSCs that perform functions requiring special treatment for DID
adequacy.
The NRC staff notes that this program, once fully developed in the OL application, would be
needed to support a regulatory finding under 10 CFR 50.34(b)(6)(iv), which is applicable at the
OL application stage. Because the applicant has not provided all of the required information on
the RAM program in its CP application and is not seeking to demonstrate compliance with this
regulation at the CP application stage, the NRC staff is not making any regulatory findings
pertaining to this section. The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 8.10.2, which discussed the
RAM program degradation mechanism assessment and finds that using XI.2 Article VII-3 in
addition to the materials qualification methodology described in PSAR section 3.8 is a
reasonable approach. The NRC staff will evaluate the RAM program as part of the OL
application review, including the basis and acceptability of the departure from the scope of
ASME Section XI-2 as endorsed in RG 1.246 (PSAR section 8.2), which includes passive SSCs
that perform functions requiring special treatment for DID adequacy.
